basis: Independently curated original deck retained in full, with original note-based additions reviewed against the subject specification. External notes supply coverage prompts, not verbatim cards.

base_cards.front: What is a genome?
back: An organism’s entire genetic material.

base_cards.front: Which division produces gametes?
back: Meiosis.

base_cards.front: How many chromosomes are usually present in a human gamete?
What is an allele?
back: A version of a gene.

base_cards.front: What does heterozygous mean?
back: Having two different alleles for a gene.

base_cards.front: What is the phenotype?
back: The expressed characteristics of an organism.

base_cards.front: Which base pairs with adenine in DNA?
back: Thymine.

base_cards.front: Name the cell structure where proteins are synthesised.
back: Ribosome.

base_cards.front: What is a mutation?
back: A change in DNA.

base_cards.front: What is a clone?
back: An organism genetically identical to its source organism.

base_cards.front: Which two classification levels form a binomial name?
back: Genus and species.

base_cards.front: Who developed the three-domain system?
back: Carl Woese.

base_cards.front: Compare sexual and asexual reproduction.
back: Sexual reproduction involves **fusion of gametes** and mixes genetic information.
Asexual reproduction uses **one parent without gamete fusion**, producing genetically identical offspring apart from mutations.

base_cards.front: Why can asexual reproduction be advantageous in stable conditions?
back: There is **no need to find a mate**, so reproduction can be rapid.
Successful genetic characteristics are preserved, allowing many offspring when conditions remain suitable.

base_cards.front: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of sexual reproduction.
back: Genetic **variation** increases the chance some offspring survive environmental change.
Finding a mate and producing gametes can cost time and energy.

base_cards.front: Describe how strawberries and daffodils reproduce asexually.
back: Strawberries produce **runners** that grow into new plants.
Daffodils produce **bulbs** that develop into new plants.

base_cards.front: How do malaria parasites demonstrate both reproductive methods?
back: They reproduce **asexually in the human host**.
Their **sexual stage occurs in the mosquito**.

base_cards.front: Explain how a gene differs from a chromosome.
back: A gene is a **section of DNA coding for an amino-acid sequence** used in a protein.
A chromosome is a long DNA molecule carrying **many genes**.

base_cards.front: Describe the components of a DNA nucleotide.
back: A nucleotide contains a **sugar and phosphate**.
It also contains **one of four bases**.

base_cards.front: Explain why amino-acid order matters in a protein.
back: The order affects how the protein **folds into a particular shape**.
Shape determines function, for example whether an enzyme’s **active site** fits its substrate.

base_cards.front: Give two ways studying the human genome can be useful.
back: Identify genes linked to **inherited disorders**, supporting understanding or treatment.
Compare genetic information to trace **human migration** and relationships.

base_cards.front: Distinguish genotype from phenotype using a simple allele example.
back: **Genotype** is the allele combination, for example Aa.
**Phenotype** is the expressed characteristic; Aa expresses the dominant characteristic in this simple model.

base_cards.front: Why can unaffected parents have a child with a recessive disorder?
back: Both parents can be **heterozygous carriers**.
The child can inherit the **recessive allele from each parent**, becoming homozygous recessive.

base_cards.front: Give a genetic cause and an environmental cause of variation.
back: Genetic: different **alleles inherited from parents**, or a mutation.
Environmental: different nutrition, training or exposure to sunlight.

base_cards.front: Explain why height is not a simple one-gene characteristic.
back: Many **genes** influence height.
**Environmental factors**, such as childhood nutrition, also affect the phenotype.

base_cards.front: Explain one risk of inbreeding during selective breeding.
back: Close relatives are more likely to share harmful **recessive alleles**.
Offspring are more likely to inherit two copies and express the disorder.

base_cards.front: Why are antibiotics ineffective against viruses?
back: Antibiotics act on bacterial structures or processes.
Viruses reproduce inside host cells and do not have the same antibiotic targets.

base_cards.front: Give two reasons the fossil record is incomplete.
back: Many early organisms were **soft-bodied**, leaving few preserved remains.
Geological activity destroyed or altered many remains, and many fossils have not been found.

base_cards.front: Give two possible causes of extinction.
back: Rapid environmental change or a new disease can prevent survival/reproduction.
New predators or competitors can reduce food or survival until no individuals remain.

base_cards.front: In a tree, A and B share a more recent ancestor than A and C. Explain which are more closely related.
back: **A and B** are more closely related.
They share the **more recent common ancestor**, not merely neighbouring names on the diagram.

base_cards.front: Explain how meiosis and fertilisation maintain chromosome number across generations.
back: Meiosis **halves the chromosome number**, producing gametes with 23 chromosomes in humans.
Fertilisation joins two gamete nuclei.
The fertilised egg has **46 chromosomes**, restoring the usual body-cell number.

base_cards.front: Describe chromosome changes during meiosis without naming its phases.
back: DNA is **copied once**, giving joined copies of each chromosome.
The cell **divides twice**, producing four gametes with half the original chromosome number.
The gametes are **genetically different** because information from the two parents is reshuffled.

base_cards.front: Explain how a coding mutation can change enzyme activity.
back: A changed base sequence can change the **amino-acid sequence**.
This can change folding and **active-site shape**.
Substrate may bind less effectively, changing the reaction rate; not every mutation has this effect.

base_cards.front: Explain how a non-coding DNA variant can affect a phenotype.
back: Some non-coding DNA helps control **gene expression**.
A variant can alter how much or when a gene is expressed.
A changed amount of a protein can alter a characteristic without changing its amino-acid sequence.

base_cards.front: Two cystic-fibrosis carriers have genotypes Cc. Determine the probability their child is affected.
back: Each parent produces gametes **C or c**.
The combinations are **CC, Cc, Cc, cc**.
Only cc is affected: **1/4 = 25%** for each pregnancy.

base_cards.front: A heterozygous parent has polydactyly, Pp. The other parent is pp. Determine the chance of an affected child.
back: Parent gametes are **P or p**, and **p only**.
Offspring combinations are **Pp, Pp, pp, pp**.
P is dominant, so **2/4 = 50%** are predicted to be affected.

base_cards.front: Use the usual XX/XY model to explain equal probabilities of female and male offspring.
back: Egg gametes carry **X**; sperm carry **X or Y**.
Fusion produces **XX or XY** with equal chances in the model.
Each outcome has probability **1/2**, not a guarantee of equal numbers in a family.

base_cards.front: In 200 children from carrier-by-carrier crosses, calculate the expected number of affected children and explain why observed numbers might differ.
back: Recessive affected probability = **1/4**.
Expected number = 200 ×1/4 = **50**.
Inheritance is **random**, so observed counts can differ from the expectation.

base_cards.front: Describe three different ways fossils can form.
back: Hard parts can be **replaced by minerals**.
Remains can persist where **decay is prevented**, such as amber or ice.
Traces such as footprints or burrows can be preserved.

base_cards.front: Why was Darwin’s theory initially difficult for some people to accept?
back: It challenged the belief that species were **created unchanged**.
There was **insufficient evidence** available at first.
The mechanism of **inheritance and variation** was not yet understood.

base_cards.front: Explain why Mendel’s work was not immediately recognised.
back: His pea-plant results suggested inherited **units**, before genes were known.
Chromosomes and their role in inheritance were not yet understood.
Later discoveries provided a mechanism and evidence supporting his explanation.

base_cards.front: State the three domains and give the distinguishing cell-type relationship.
back: **Archaea:** a distinct prokaryotic domain, including many organisms from extreme environments.
**Bacteria:** the bacterial prokaryotic domain.
**Eukaryota:** organisms with eukaryotic cells, including animals, plants, fungi and protists.

base_cards.front: Describe the main steps linking a DNA base sequence to a functional protein.
back: A base sequence provides the **code for amino-acid order**; three bases code for an amino acid.
A template reaches a **ribosome**.
Carrier molecules bring amino acids, which join in the specified order.
The chain **folds into a particular shape**, enabling its function.

base_cards.front: Explain how natural selection can make a camouflaged insect colour more common.
back: A population contains **inherited variation** in colour.
Better-camouflaged insects are less likely to be eaten.
They are more likely to **survive and reproduce**.
Their offspring inherit the alleles, so these alleles become **more common over generations**.

base_cards.front: Explain how isolation can lead to a new species.
back: Populations become **isolated**, preventing breeding between them.
Different conditions and mutations produce different variation and selection pressures.
Over many generations different alleles accumulate.
Eventually the populations cannot interbreed to produce **fertile offspring**, so they are different species.

base_cards.front: Describe selective breeding to produce wheat with high yield and disease resistance.
back: Choose parents showing the **desired characteristics**.
Breed them together.
Select offspring with the best combination and breed those offspring.
Repeat selection and breeding over **many generations**, rather than simply reusing the original parents.

base_cards.front: Describe how bacteria can be genetically engineered to produce human insulin.
back: Use enzymes to **isolate the human insulin gene**.
Cut a **plasmid vector** and insert the gene.
Transfer the modified plasmid into bacterial cells.
Grow the bacteria so they express the gene and produce insulin, which is collected and purified.

base_cards.front: Describe adult-cell cloning and identify the source of the clone’s nuclear DNA.
back: Remove the nucleus from an **unfertilised egg**.
Insert an **adult body-cell nucleus**.
Use an electric stimulus to start division, then transfer the embryo to a host uterus.
The clone’s **nuclear DNA comes from the adult nucleus donor**.

base_cards.front: Compare plant cuttings, tissue culture and embryo splitting.
back: A cutting grows into a plant from a portion of a parent plant.
Tissue culture uses **small groups of cells**, nutrients and hormones to grow many plants.
Embryo splitting separates cells from an early animal embryo for transfer into host mothers.
Each makes genetically identical offspring from its source, but uses a different starting material.

base_cards.front: Explain how antibiotic-resistant bacteria become more common during treatment.
back: A **random mutation** can make some bacteria resistant.
Antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria while resistant ones survive.
Survivors reproduce rapidly and pass on resistance.
Resistant bacteria form a **larger proportion** of the population; antibiotic does not deliberately create a useful mutation.

base_cards.front: Describe how evidence helped classification develop beyond physical resemblance alone.
back: Linnaeus grouped organisms by observable characteristics.
Improved microscopes revealed more detail about cell structures.
Biochemical and genetic evidence revealed deeper relationships.
Woese’s **three-domain system** separates Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota using such evidence.

additions.front: Why is a gene not the same as one triplet of DNA bases?
back: A gene contains a sequence of many bases specifying an amino-acid sequence. One triplet specifies one amino acid in the course model.

additions.front: How can inserting one base affect more than one amino acid?
back: It can shift how later bases are grouped into triplets, changing the later code.

additions.front: Must a substitution change the protein’s function?
back: No. It may code for the same amino acid or cause a change with little effect on folding or function.

additions.front: How can a non-coding variant affect phenotype?
back: It can alter gene expression and the amount of protein made, without changing that protein’s sequence.

additions.front: What can be inferred from two unaffected parents having a child with a simple recessive condition?
back: Both parents must be carriers in that model.

additions.front: Can two parents with a dominant condition have an unaffected child?
back: Yes, if both are heterozygous. Their child can inherit the recessive allele from each parent.

additions.front: For two carriers, what is the probability of two affected children in two independent conceptions?
back: 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Each individual conception still has a 1/4 probability.

additions.front: Does a dominant phenotype identify the exact genotype?
back: No. In the simple model it may result from either a homozygous dominant or heterozygous genotype.

additions.front: What is copied before meiosis, and what is halved in the resulting gametes?
back: DNA is copied before division. The two divisions produce gametes with half the original chromosome number.

additions.front: Why does a human insulin gene not turn a bacterium into a human cell?
back: It supplies instructions for that protein, rather than transferring the entire human genome and cell organisation.

additions.front: How does cloning differ from genetic engineering?
back: Cloning copies an existing genotype. Genetic engineering changes a genome by introducing a selected gene.

additions.front: Why can DNA evidence change a classification based on appearance?
back: Similar appearance can evolve under similar pressures. Molecular comparisons can reveal different ancestry.

additions.front: Does the horizontal position of a species on a tree show how evolved it is?
back: No. Relationships depend on shared branch points, not where the label is placed.

additions.front: When can branch length on an evolutionary tree be interpreted as time?
back: When the tree supplies an appropriate time scale. It should not be assumed for every diagram.

additions.front: Does rearranging branches around a shared join change ancestry?
back: No. The same connections still represent the same common ancestors.

additions.front: Why is a genetically uniform crop not the same as conserving genetic diversity?
back: Many cloned individuals may all carry the same variants. Their number can increase without increasing the variety of alleles.
